summary: This proposed standard defines a way to transport OSPFv3 packets over IPv4. Combined with the existing OSPFv3 Address Family extension, it can simplify moving from an IPv4-only OSPFv2 routing domain to a dual-stack OSPFv3 domain. It also updates RFC 5838 to support virtual links in the IPv4 unicast address family.

plainLanguage.summary: Moving from an old road system to a new one is easier if the new trucks can still use the old roads for a while. This lets the newer routing system run over older roads during the switch.

questions: which ip protocol number does ospf use
does ospfv3 over ipv4 support virtual links
subtitle: Carry OSPFv3 packets inside plain IPv4, so a network can start its move to IPv6 routing before every device speaks IPv6.

tldr.problem: Moving from an IPv4-only OSPFv2 network to OSPFv3 normally needs IPv6 on every link, but some deployed link-layer equipment only supports IPv4 and ARP, or IPv4 over PPP.
tldr.mechanism: OSPFv3 packets are placed directly in an IPv4 packet with protocol number 89, starting with an OSPF header whose version field is 3. Combined with the OSPFv3 address family extension, one OSPFv3 process can serve the move to dual-stack.
tldr.outcome: Networks can deploy and test OSPFv3 over IPv4 now and later move to OSPFv3 over IPv6. The RFC also updates RFC 5838 so virtual links work in the IPv4 unicast address family.

today: RFC 7949 is a Proposed Standard from August 2016 that updates RFC 5838. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Using OSPFv3 Over IPv4
sections.content:
OSPF is an interior gateway routing protocol. OSPFv2 (RFC 2328) is the version deployed over IPv4, and OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) is the version deployed over IPv6. OSPFv3 also supports multiple address families (RFC 5838), including both the IPv6 unicast and the IPv4 unicast address family.

Because of that, OSPFv3 can be deployed over IPv4 without any changes to either OSPFv3 or IPv4. During the move to IPv6, future OSPF extensions can focus on OSPFv3, and OSPFv2 can move to maintenance mode.

The mechanism works because OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 share the same IP protocol number, 89, and both put the OSPF version field at the same offset in the packet header.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers use OSPF to tell each other which roads exist. This RFC says the newer OSPF can send its messages inside the older kind of envelope, so the switch can happen step by step.

sections.title: Why IPv4-Only Links Matter
sections.content:
OSPFv3 only needs IPv6 link-local addresses to form adjacencies, but IPv6 over Ethernet uses a different EtherType (0x86dd) from IPv4 (0x0800) and ARP (0x0806). Some deployed link-layer equipment has hardware filters keyed on the EtherType, so IPv6 framing for OSPFv3 will not pass. In other cases PPP over a serial interface may carry only IPv4.

The RFC gives satellite (SATCOM) and VSAT links, used by banks and retailers to reach branches and stores, as places where such equipment is common. These deployments can run OSPFv3 over IPv4 today and move to OSPFv3 over IPv6 after equipment is upgraded. The RFC says this can cost less to operate than running OSPFv2 and then attempting a flag-day switch to OSPFv3.

It also covers uneven networks. If the IPv4 deployment is a superset of the IPv6 one, OSPFv3 is expected to travel over IPv4. If the IPv6 deployment is the larger one, it is expected to travel over IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old network boxes only understand one kind of envelope. Using that kind lets them join in now, and they can switch to the new envelope when they get replaced.

sections.title: Encapsulation in IPv4
sections.content:
An OSPFv3 packet is carried directly as the payload of an IPv4 packet, without an IPv6 header. The IPv4 protocol field is 89, and the payload starts with the OSPF packet header with its version field set to 3. An OSPF link-local signaling (LLS) data block (RFC 5613) may trail the OSPFv3 packet.

An IPv4 header without options is 20 octets, shorter than an IPv6 header. So the link MTU that is enough for IPv6 is enough for OSPFv3 in a 20-octet IPv4 header. If the MTU is still not enough, OSPFv3 can rely on IP fragmentation and reassembly.
sections.plainLanguage: The OSPFv3 message goes in an IPv4 envelope marked 89 so the receiver knows it is routing mail. The IPv4 envelope is a bit smaller than the IPv6 one, so it fits.

sections.title: Source and Destination Addresses
sections.content:
The source address is the primary IPv4 address of the sending interface, and all OSPFv3 routers on the link should share the same IPv4 subnet. An implementation MAY support adjacencies with neighbors on different IPv4 subnets. If it does, the IPv4 data plane MUST resolve addresses using ARP on multi-access networks and point-to-point over LAN (RFC 5309) for direct next hops on different subnets, and BFD cannot be used for adjacency loss detection.

The destination is either an IPv4 multicast address or the neighbor's IPv4 unicast address. Packets for AllSPFRouters MUST use 224.0.0.5 and packets for AllDRouters MUST use 224.0.0.6. A unicast packet uses the neighbor's IPv4 address.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router writes its own IPv4 address as the sender. Messages for everyone go to a shared group address, and private messages go to the neighbor's own address.

sections.title: The OSPFv3 Header Checksum
sections.content: For IPv4 transport, the pseudo-header used in the checksum contains the IPv4 source and destination addresses, the OSPFv3 protocol ID and the OSPFv3 packet length taken from the OSPFv3 header (Appendix A.3.1 of RFC 5340). The layout is similar to the UDP pseudo-header in RFC 768: two 32-bit addresses, then a zero octet, the protocol value 89 and a 16-bit length.
sections.plainLanguage: The checksum is a quick check number. It also looks at the sender and receiver addresses, so a message that landed in the wrong place is caught.

sections.title: Virtual Links
sections.content:
A virtual link may connect routers that are not directly attached, so the destination must be a reachable unicast address for the far endpoint. RFC 5838 restricted virtual links to the IPv6 address family because an IPv4 destination was not routable there.

With IPv4 transport, virtual links can be supported for IPv4 address families by setting the destination to a reachable IPv4 unicast address of the endpoint. This relaxes the restriction in Section 2.8 of RFC 5838, as long as the transport is also IPv4. If IPv4 transport is used for IPv6 address families, virtual links cannot be supported. In domains that require virtual links, the IP transport MUST match the address family.
sections.plainLanguage: A virtual link is like a tunnel between two routers that are not neighbors. It now works for IPv4 routes too, as long as the tunnel uses IPv4 as well.

sections.title: Coexistence With OSPFv2
sections.content:
OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 over IPv4 use exactly the same protocol number and IPv4 addresses, so a packet for one may be delivered to the other's process. The mismatched packet is dropped after the version in the first octet of the header is checked. Standard sockets still deliver a copy to each matching socket, so the right process also gets it.

Implementations SHOULD keep separate counters for protocol mismatches and SHOULD let operators suppress the SNMP bad-packet notifications (ospfIfRxBadPacket, ospfVirtIfRxBadPacket, ospfv3IfRxBadPacket and ospv3VirtIfRxBadPacket) when an OSPFv2 packet reaches OSPFv3 or the reverse.
sections.plainLanguage: Two mail clerks share one mailbox, so each sometimes gets the other's letters. They just hand the wrong ones back, and nobody should sound an alarm about it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
OSPFv3 relies on IPsec for authentication and confidentiality, and RFC 4552 describes that for IPv6 transport. For IPv4 transport, further work such as the draft "Authentication/Confidentiality for OSPFv2" would be required.

The OSPFv3 Authentication Trailer (RFC 7166) is an alternative that works inside OSPFv3 itself. With IPv4 encapsulation, the IPv4 source address goes in the first 4 octets of Apad, followed by 0x878FE1F3 repeated (L-4)/4 times, where L is the hash length in octets. Otherwise generating and validating the trailer does not change.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking the messages needs a lock that fits the IPv4 envelope. This RFC points to one lock that already works and says the other still needs more work.
